Harry Potter nerds have forced an undersea cable to be moved to avoid Dobby the house elf's grave, now runs close to Bronze Age remains instead
summary: "The whole thing is fictitious, what are you talking about?"
body: An undersea power cable linking the UK National Grid to Ireland has been forced to relocate, after Harry Potter fans complained it would go through Dobby's grave. You know, Dobby the house elf . The fictional character created by J.K. Rowling. Fans became aware of the desecration of Dobby's memorial after a BBC interview with project manager Simon Ludlam, who detailed plans to put the cable underground at Freshwater West beach in Wales (via The Guardian ). This just happens to be the location where Dobby's fictional death was shot for Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 1 , and the site of a fan-made shrine. According to Ludlam: "We did the [BBC] shot, we finished, I went back to London, and they then aired it a couple of weeks later. And we got hundreds of calls, I mean, hundreds of calls." Ludlam doesn't appear to be a Harry Potter fan, as he expressed confusion over all the fuss created by the location. A colleague told him "Apparently, we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave." "Dobby, who's Dobby?" Ludlam recounts. "He's a fictitious character in a fictious book.... what are you taking about?" His colleague told him: "Not, it's very, very serious." (Image credi…

title: Saber CEO hides jab at Randy Pitchford in game trailer as payback for Pitchford dumping on Embracer: 'Without Embracer, Randy is performing magic tricks at birthday parties for a living'
summary: I love low-stakes drama.
body: If you watched the recent trailer for Saber Interactive's upcoming Rideshare 'Stimulator' (the quotation marks are part of the title) you may have thought it seemed a little bit hinky in spots. Midway through the video, after a quick rundown of some of the game's oddball passengers, the narrator says, "And when I think I've met the randiest of passengers, someone even stranger gets it." First of all, who says "randy"—a synonym, mostly British, for "horny"—anymore, aside from people in those cozy English countryside murder mystery TV shows my mom likes? And second, where are these randy people to begin with? Nobody in the video looks all that revved up to me. A few seconds later, another oddity: A personalized Texas license plate, not zoomed in enough to be conspicuous but clear enough to read without trouble: USB DRV. And there's sort of a gear-looking thing on it too, not the sort of symbol traditionally associated with the Lone Star State. (Image credit: Unigine) It's something I would never have picked up on, because I tend to not pay much attention to what's going on around me. Fortunately, Stephen Totilo at Game File did notice, and he asked Saber Interactive CEO Matt Kartch …

title: Mark Zuckerberg's rambling AI manifesto is 6,434 words of high-handed platitudes and dubious conclusions
summary: Tell us what you really think. No actually, don't.
body: I've spent a large part of my morning reading the words of Mark Zuckerberg. 6,434 of them, to be precise, if we're including the "Mark" signoff at the bottom. The Meta CEO (and everyone's favourite smart glasses advocate ) has written what can only be described as a manifesto regarding upcoming "superintelligent" AI technology—and I'll be honest, my eyes have glazed over more than once. The piece/blog post/rambling diatribe has been posted on Meta's website, under the title " The Future is for Everyone: The Path to a Positive AI Future ." If you'll allow me, I'd like to quote some choice insights: "The defining questions of our age are who will have access to superintelligence and what will we direct it towards. Will it be centralized and restricted to a few institutions, or will it be a tool that empowers everyone?" asks Zuckerberg. "We propose a philosophy based on individual empowerment as the source of prosperity, invention as the primary purpose of superintelligence, and balance of power as the foundation of safety." body: Asus Armoury Crate is not my favourite bit of software. It looks all high-tech on the surface, but any time I use it for more than five minutes, I'm reminded of the fact it's rather messy. title: GTA 6 might not technically be $100, but it's had its cake and ate it too as pre-orders are 'skewing more to the premium edition'
summary: Schrodinger's price change.
body: Grand Theft Auto 6's potential price-point was a thing of much consternation in the lead-up to its reveal. Months of rumours —and even the Bank of America getting involved in the discourse, because why not—led to the question: Are they really gonna charge $100 for this thing? You're reading this article because they didn't, but you're also reading this article because they sort of did. See, GTA 6 has both an $80 version and a $100 version, the latter of which hides some potentially major parts of its identity behind the upgrade , including a handful of stores that may very well remind you that you've not shelled out every time you go near them. There's this itchy capitalist feeling that Rockstar probably did actually want to charge a hundo for the thing, but didn't, because that'd have gamers up in arms—as it turns out, that might've been the smart play. title: As if PCs weren't expensive enough already, Microsoft is reportedly now charging OEMs more for Windows licenses

body: Taiwanese news site United Daily News reports that, according to one source, Microsoft is charging Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) significantly more for Windows licensing fees this year than in previous years (via Wccftech ). These are the fees that PC makers, for instance, must pay to Microsoft to package their machines with the operating system. UDN says (via machine translation): "A PC brand executive stated that Microsoft increases licensing fees for Windows OEMs every year. In the past, licensing fees mostly increased by single digits each year, but starting in July this year, the average increase has reached 7% to 10%, which is a significant increase compared to previous years." I can't confirm whether UDN's source is correct, but given Framework recently said it's seen an increase in Windows license costs , I have no reason to doubt it. Apparently Microsoft charges OEMs more for Windows licenses if they're used with higher-end CPUs—which seems like a strange decision to me given it shouldn't actually change anything about the operating system being delivered, but I'm not a business bigwig so what do I know? title: Firefox stunts on Edge as Microsoft gears up to neuter adblockers: 'uBlock Origin isn't going anywhere'
summary: Blocked. Blocked. Blocked. None of these corpo browsers are free of sin.
body: Earlier this year, Google Chrome annoyed a whole lot of adblock users by killing support for Manifest V2 extensions . It's a Manifest V3 world now, which means the permissions and APIs that thoroughgoing adblockers like uBlock Origin rely on are a thing of the past on Chrome (it's since been replaced by a pared-down version: uBlock Origin Lite ). Now, Microsoft Edge is following suit: "Over the next few months, MV2 extensions will be gradually turned off by default," says Redmond . All of which is red meat for the folks over at Mozilla Firefox, the free-and-open-source browser that once reigned supreme on our PCs before Chrome came and ate its lunch. In posts across social media, Firefox kicked Edge (and Chrome) in their self-inflicted bruises, declaring that "Our support for uBlock Origin isn't going anywhere", a post that came days after it wrote "Reminder that you can still just… use ad blockers on Firefox. Wild concept, we know." Now, like I said, it's not like Chromium-based browsers are murdering adblockers wholesale. body: At the end of last month, id Software lead services programmer Chris Hayes offered a blunt appraisal of Xbox's management during an interview with YouTube channel Auf ein Bier, saying Microsoft's repeated mass layoffs have proved that its leadership "fundamentally don't understand art." Elsewhere in the interview, Hayes expanded the scope of his criticism beyond the immediate damage wrought by the latest round of Xbox cuts . Looking at the industry more broadly, Hayes, who's still a Microsoft employee, says mass layoffs and nearsighted cost cutting are producing worse games, because they're denying game developers the opportunity—and motivation—to improve their craft. While major companies like Microsoft might brag about the "great IPs and studios" that they own, Hayes said they seem incapable of understanding that they regularly harm their own capability to produce anything of value with those brands and developers. title: 'Thank you so much for the best weekend ever': The id Software gang got together at QuakeCon, and it sure looks like everyone had a great time
summary: I love a happy ending.
body: The recently concluded QuakeCon was a big one, marking the 30th anniversary of the game that started it all and, more notably, bringing id Software co-founders Adrian Carmack, John Carmack, Tom Hall, and John Romero together for the first time in a very long time. I had wondered, in the lead-up to the event, if it might get a little awkward or uncomfortable: Differences between the Johns were " over-dramatized " over the years, according to Romero Games co-founder Brenda Romero, but Adrian Carmack filed a lawsuit over his removal from the studio back in 2005, and other internal conflicts over the years led to the dismissal of well-liked employees like American McGee and Paul Steed. The more recent layoffs of Xbox that left the studio in varying states of " gutted ," depending on who you ask, also threatened to overshadow the whole thing. So, you know: you wonder . Now that everything is wrapped up, I'm happy to report that if there was any awkwardness or discomfort between the studio's famed founders, everyone kept it to themselves and they all seemed to have a really good time. "QuakeCon was fantastic this year, especially reuniting with the original founders!" John Carmack wrote…

title: Corsair isn't rolling in money from its mega-expensive RAM kits—and it's all thanks to higher component costs and lower demand
summary: The memory crisis is a complicated beast.
body: If you've looked at memory prices recently, you've probably seen Corsair DIMMs selling for astonishing prices. The 32 GB Vengeance DDR5 RGB kit sitting in my PC right now is selling for $480 at Amazon , whereas I bought it for $90-$100 just a couple of years ago. Corsair RAM can still be some of the cheapest comparatively , but it's very pricey nonetheless. So, Corsair must be raking in money hand over fist, right? Not quite, at least according to its recent filings with the SEC . The figures show a ~9% decline in Q2 2026 gaming component and system revenue overall compared to last year—although gross profit was up 17%. Memory revenue itself has increased, but its "other component products" revenue has decreased significantly. According to the company: "We are both a seller of memory products and a purchaser of memory and other components from third-party suppliers. As a result, elevated pricing benefits net sales and margin on the memory products we sell, while also increasing our cost of components across our broader product offerings." Corsair sells memory, but doesn't manufacture the actual modules themselves, sourcing them instead from Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron (plus CXMT…
